title: Getting argparse to manage arguments with multiple names?
author: HippoMan
bschubert
text:
ArgumentParser.add_argument accepts multiple flag names as the first argument(s). Does this do what you’re looking for?
>>> parser.add_argument('-o', '-O', '--outfile', '--outputfile', '--output', '--out')

>>> parser.parse_args(['--output', 'foo'])
Namespace(outfile='foo')
>>> parser.parse_args(['-O', 'foo'])
Namespace(outfile='foo')

author: HippoMan
text:

Ah … thank you.

author: bschubert
text:
Hippo Man:

but the multiple parser.parse_args calls are still inconvenient.


To be clear, you don’t need to call parse_args multiple times. Those two lines were just to show that the same parser will handle either flag name.

author: HippoMan
text:
Hippo Man:

parser.parse_args([‘-o’, ‘-O’, ‘–outputfile’, ‘–outfile’, ‘–output’, ‘–out’, ‘foo’])


I unexpectedly got an opportunity to try this on the computer just now. And it fails as follows:
: error: argument -o/-O/--outputfile/--outfile/--output/--out: expected one argument
So indeed I would have to make multiple parser.parse_args() calls in order to enable the argument-parsing functionality that I describe above.
It’s sad (at least for me) that argparse requires this extra verbosity in order to accomplish this.
If I use getopt instead of argparse, I can do the following:
    opts, args = getopt.getopt(
        sys.argv[1:],
        'o:O:',
        [ 'outputfile=', 'outfile=', 'output=', 'out=' ]
    )
    for o, a in opts:
        if o in ( '-o', '-O', '--outputfile', '--outfile', '--output', '--out' ):
            foo = a
To me, this is less objectionable than the argparse methodology. Nonethless, argparse offers more capabilities than getopt, so like I wrote above, now I think that I’m just going to bite the bullet and settle for argparse anyway.

author: svioletg
text:
You could do this by passing nargs='?', which makes it so that argument accepts either no values or a single value:
from argparse import ArgumentParser

parser = ArgumentParser()
parser.add_argument('-o', '-O', '--outputfile', '--outfile', '--output', '--out', dest='outfile', nargs='?')

args = parser.parse_args(['-o', '-O', '--outputfile', '--outfile', '--output', '--out', '1'])
outfile = args.outfile[-1] # equals '1'

Although this makes it so that a value isn’t required at any point, so you’d have to check the length of args.outfile and handle it being empty accordingly.
I am admittedly curious what use case you have for this, though.

author: cheviot
text:
That error means that argparse expected a value after the flag, and there wasn’t one. You’ve provided a list of flags, all of which are missing a value apart from the last one i.e. '--out', 'foo'
You mentioned you want to invoke this from the command line, so there’s no need to supply anything to parse_args() - just define them all in one call to add_argument(), then parse. This seems to work fine for me:
# arg_demo.py
import argparse

if __name__ == "__main__":
    parser = argparse.ArgumentParser()
    parser.add_argument(
        "-o", "-O", "--outfile", "--outputfile", "--output", "--out"
    )
    args = parser.parse_args()
    print(args)

$ python arg_demo.py 
Namespace(outfile=None)

$ python arg_demo.py -o FOO
Namespace(outfile='FOO')

$ python arg_demo.py -O BAR
Namespace(outfile='BAR')

Matt:

You mentioned you want to invoke this from the command line, so there’s no need to supply anything to parse_args() - just define them all in one call to add_argument(), then parse. This seems to work fine for me:


Ah! Now I see from your example above that the name of the variable that will get set in the program if any of the flags appear on the command line is the name of the first flag in the list which begins with a double-hyphen: ‘–outfile’ in this case.
And I now therefore understand that if instead, I code the argument list as follows …

… then the name of the variable that will get set in the program if any of the flags appear on the command line will be “out”.
This is indeed straightforward and doesn’t require all of the argparse verbiage that I mistakenly thought that I needed.
Thank you very much! This answers my question, and now I see that argparse isn’t objectionable like I previously thought.

author: HippoMan

Violet:

I am admittedly curious what use case you have for this, though.


I want to be able to write python programs which can accept several different versions of command-line flags, but always set the same python variable in the program when any of these flags are given, no matter which version of the flag might appear on the command line.
In other words, using the example that I gave above, I would always want the value “the-output-file” to be put into a python variable specifically named “outfile”, no matter which of the six following invocations of my script might be performed:

myscript -O the-output-file
myscript --outfile the-output-file
myscript --output the-output-file
myscript --outputfile the-output-file
myscript --out the-output-file


And I want this to be done without lots of argparse verbiage.

So, now I feel comfortable using argparse, after all.

author: svioletg
text: If I’m not mistaken, how argparse picks which name to use on the resulting object from parser.parse_args() is it uses the first long-form option given if present, or if no long names are given it uses the first short one (-s, --start outputs to start, -s, -S outputs to s, --start, -s outputs to start…), but something useful to remember in cases like this is the dest option to add_argument(), which lets you explicitly give a destination name for that option. e.g. parser.add_argument('-o', '--output', dest='outfile') after parsing will have that option’s value available at args.outfile, regardless of the option strings given.

author: HippoMan
text: Thank very much for explaining the ‘dest’ option. Now I see how to accomplish what I want, even if there are no long-form arguments.

author: adrianofdoom
text:
Here’s how I do it
These are methods from a class
def _parse_args(self):
    """
    _parse_args parse command line args
    """
    parser = argparse.ArgumentParser(
        epilog="scte35inject is part of threefive.\n\n"
    )
    parser.add_argument(
        "-i",
        "--input",
        "-I",
        "--INPUT",
        default=sys.stdin.buffer,
        help=""" Input source, like "/home/a/vid.ts"
                                or "udp://@235.35.3.5:3535"
                                [default: sys.stdin.buffer]
                                """,
    )
 
    parser.add_argument(
        "-t",
        "--time_signals",
        action="store_const",
        default=False,
        const=True,
        help="Flag to insert Time Signal cues at iframes.",
    )

    args = parser.parse_args()
    self._apply_args(args)

def _apply_args(self, args):
    """
    _apply_args applies command line args
    """
    self.infile = args.input
    self.time_signals = args.time_signals

I use the _apply_args method to map the args to a var, but dest sounds good too. I was unaware of dest.
